Touring on her new album "Luck... or Something," the 38-year-old former Disney star makes her first Michigan concert appearance since 2005, which already has many millennials melting down. (Aug. 15, Pine Knob)

5. My Chemical Romance

The emo rockers return to the road for a second summer of stadium shows backing their 2006 album "The Black Parade," which turns 20 in October. As a special treat for the Detroit crowd, Iggy Pop — a longtime influence on My Chem — will open the show like no other 79-year-old can. (Aug. 21, Comerica Park)

6. Bruno Mars

The pop showstopper is back with a new album — "The Romantic" was released earlier this year — and will be performing his first Detroit shows since a two-night stand at Little Caesars Arena in 2018. (May 9-10 at Ford Field)

7. Foo Fighters

Dave Grohl and company come rocking into town for their first local concert in six years, and their first-ever Detroit stadium concert. Queens of the Stone Age open. (Aug. 6, Ford Field)

8. Usher/ Chris Brown

Two R&B superstars, one night. Usher and Chris Brown join forces for their joint "R&B Tour" — their last names are Raymond and Brown, get it? — which hits the Detroit Lions' home just before the 4th of July. (July 2-3, Ford Field)

9. Morgan Wallen

The country megastar plays back-to-back nights at the Big House, the second and third concerts hosted at Michigan Stadium, following last year's record-breaking inaugural show from Zach Bryan. (July 24-25, Michigan Stadium)

10. Yungblud

The 28-year-old up-and-comer opens this year's outdoor concert season with this Michigan Lottery Amphitheatre headlining show, the kickoff of his 2026 tour, which follows a sold-out September 2025 concert at the Fillmore Detroit. (May 1, Michigan Lottery Amphitheatre)

11. Rush

The Canadian rock band's first area concerts in more than a decade (and since the 2020 death of drummer Neil Peart) come on their Fifty Something tour. (Aug. 26, 28 at Little Caesars Arena)

12. Megan Moroney

The rising Georgia country singer brings the tour behind February's "Cloud 9" to Detroit, marking her first area arena concert. JP Saxe & Solon Holt open. (Aug. 18, Little Caesars Arena)

13. J. Cole

The North Carolina rapper released his latest album, "The Fall Off," in February, and he returns to Detroit with his first area concert in five years. (Aug. 16, Little Caesars Arena)

14. TLC/ Salt-N-Pepa/ En Vogue

Sorry, no scrubs allowed at this concert. TLC returns to the area, and they bring with them a powerful all-female lineup: they'll be joined by Salt-N-Pepa, fresh off their 2025 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and '90s hitmakers En Vogue. The tour is called "It's Iconic" for a reason. (Aug. 23, Pine Knob)

15. Ed Sheeran

The last time Ed Sheeran played Ford Field, in 2023, he brought Eminem out with him on stage. He can't possibly repeat or top that magic trick — can he? (Aug. 29, Ford Field)

16. Jimmy Eat World

The reliable rock band, led by Jim Adkins, brings the tour celebrating the 25th anniversary of "Bleed American" to Michigan Lottery, along with an emo dream lineup of openers, Sunny Day Real Estate and the Get Up Kids. Get ready, it's time to feel again. (June 12, Michigan Lottery Amphitheatre)

17. Don Toliver

The Grammy-nominated Houston rapper hits the road on the tour behind his fifth album, "Octane," which was released in January. With SahBabii, SoFaygo & CHASE B. (June 4, Little Caesars Arena)

18. Chris Stapleton

The "Tennessee Whiskey" singer played Ford Field in 2024 while opening for George Strait, this time he returns to headline the building. He'll be joined by Lainey Wilson and Allen Stone. (Aug. 8, Ford Field)

19. A$AP Rocky

It's been nine years since the Harlem rapper performed in Detroit, and he returns backing his latest album, "Don't Be Dumb," on what the promotional materials are calling the "dumbest tour of all time." Well, then! (July 8, Little Caesars Arena)

20. Weezer

It's been 30 years since the release of "Pinkerton," but Weezer has so many albums that they're not commemorating any particular anniversary on this outing. Instead, this tour — which features openers The Shins and Silversun Pickups — is simply a celebration of all things Weezer. (Sept. 23, Little Caesars Arena)

21. Brooks & Dunn

The switch to the "Neon Moon" gets flipped on once again as Brooks & Dunn light up Pine Knob on a late September night. David Lee Murphy and Willow Avalon open. (Sept. 24, Pine Knob)

22. Outlaw Music Festival

Willie Nelson, skip a summer? Never. The unstoppable force, who turns 93 next week, leads another Outlaw Music Festival lineup which also includes the Avett Brothers, Lukas Nelson, Stephen Wilson Jr., Sierra Hull and Don Was & the Pan-Detroit Ensemble. (Aug. 22, Pine Knob)

23. Paul Simon

The legendary singer-songwriter's "A Quiet Celebration" tour will see him performing his 2023 album "Seven Psalms" in full, and following it up with classics and deep cuts from his decades of material. (June 20, Meadow Brook Amphitheatre)

24. John Mellencamp

The heartland rocker is touring and playing the hits, so expect to hear songs like "Jack and Diane," "Pink Houses," "Small Town," "Hurts So Good," "Authority Song," "R.O.C.K. in the U.S.A." and "Wild Nights," some of them for the first time in a long time. (July 16, Pine Knob)

25. Pussycat Dolls

The '00s pop troupe is on the road to celebrate the 20th anniversary of their debut album "PCD," and they'll be joined by openers Lil Kim and Mya. (July 1, Pine Knob)

26. Lil Wayne

The rap star and likely future Rock and Roll Hall of Famer will hit Pine Knob with his frequent partner-in-rhyme 2 Chainz, with whom he's collaborated on a pair of albums, 2016's "ColleGrove" and 2023's "Welcome 2 ColleGrove." (July 24, Pine Knob)

27. Lily Allen

The cheeky British pop singer turned heartbreak into inspiration with 2025's "West End Girl," a raw, deeply vulnerable concept album about the dissolution of her marriage to "Stranger Things" actor David Harbour, and she brings the tour behind the critically acclaimed set to the Fox. (Sept. 12, Fox Theatre)

28. Dogstar

Keanu Reeves' rock band (he plays bass) is hitting the road behind its new album, "All in Now," which is due out in May. (If you're gonna yell out stuff from the crowd, it's probably better to call out names of the band's songs than it is to scream "JOHN WIIIICK!," just sayin'.) (Aug. 22, Saint Andrew's Hall)

29. Wilco

Chicago rockers Wilco will pull from their vast catalog on this outing, billed simply and succinctly as "An Evening With Wilco." (June 13, Meadow Brook Amphitheatre)

30. Sarah McLachlan

The Canadian singer (and Lilith Fair founder!) is touring behind her 2025 album "Better Broken," and is backed by a catalog of favorites that stretches back to the early 1990s. Allison Russell will open. (July 15, Michigan Lottery Amphitheatre)

31. Madison Beer

The 27-year-old New Yorker released her third album, "Locket," in January, and it's full of electropop flourishes that are helping to fortify her rising pop star profile. (July 9, Fox Theatre)

32. Muse

The English alterna-rockers return to the area for the first time in seven years on the tour behind the band's latest album, "The Wow! Signal," which is due out June 26. (July 13, Pine Knob)

33. Luke Bryan

On summer break from his gig as an "American Idol" judge, the country singer — not to be confused with Luke Combs or Zach Bryan — hits Pine Knob for two nights of good time beer drinkin' party anthems. (July 11-12, Pine Knob)

34. The Black Crowes

The Brothers Robinson are back with a new album — "A Pound of Feathers" was released in March — and a new tour, with Texas country rockers Whiskey Myers opening. (July 18, Pine Knob)

35. Tim McGraw

The country king, who turns 59 next month, has been absent from Pine Knob since 2023, but will make up for lost time at this summer's tour stop. (Aug. 28, Pine Knob)

36. Ne-Yo/ Akon

The two R&B hitmakers — the forces behind hits such as "So Sick" and "Smack That" — combine their talents for the joint "Nights Like This" summer tour. (July 29, Pine Knob)

37. Kid Cudi

It's been 10 years since Cudder has played a concert in these parts, and the 42-year-old Cleveland native is on the road backing his 2025 album "Free." This one will serve as Pine Knob's summer opener. (May 23, Pine Knob)

38. Jimmy Buffett's Coral Reefer Band

Jimmy Buffett's backing band will attempt to "Keep The Party Going" on this aptly named tour that rolls on three years after Buffett's death. At the very least, the music's going to go down good with a margarita or two. (Aug. 1, Pine Knob)

39. Tori Amos

The alternative rock goddess is hitting the road in support of her upcoming 18th studio album, "In Times of Dragons," which is due out May 1. Bartees Strange will open. (Aug. 7, Fox Theatre)

40. Pitbull

It's always a party when Pitbull comes to town, and the Miami rapper will perform at Pine Knob on his "I'm Back" tour. Back? Pitbull never left! (Sept. 9, Pine Knob)

41. Evanescence

"Sanctuary," the band's upcoming sixth studio album, is due out June 5, and this tour stop will mark Amy Lee and company's first area stop since a 2022 visit to Pine Knob. (Aug. 2, Pine Knob)

42. Jack Johnson

The mellow guitarist, 50, is on the road supporting "SURFILMUSIC," the soundtrack to Johnson's new documentary, which chronicles his journey from surfer to acclaimed singer-songwriter. Hermanos Gutiérrez will open. (July 10, Pine Knob)

43. Jack Harlow

The Kentucky rapper switched things up on his new album "Monica," embracing R&B rather than the hip-hop sound that made him famous, a shift that befits the smaller, more intimate venues hosting his upcoming summer tour. (Aug. 11, Fillmore Detroit)

44. Sammy Hagar

Ageless rocker Sammy Hagar — he's 78, somehow — keeps the party going on his summer outing, which will find him playing all manner of hits from his decades-long career. Opener Rick Springfield will provide several more hits to add to the evening. (June 19, Pine Knob)

45. Rob Zombie/ Marilyn Manson

Rob Zombie's got a new album out called "The Great Satan," and it's amazing it's taken him this long to make an album called "The Great Satan." He's taking it on the road for a run of dates with his old tourmate/ sparring partner Marilyn Manson. Expect no shortage of pyro. (Sept. 4, Pine Knob)

46. Avenged Sevenfold

The California metal band is hitting the road this summer with fellow rockers Good Charlotte, a double bill of heavily tattooed '00s rock and roll. (Aug. 4, Pine Knob)

47. Bleachers

Jack Antonoff's underdog rock band heads to town on the band's "Bleachers Forever" tour, bringing the sounds of New Jersey to Sterling Heights. (Sept. 29, Michigan Lottery Amphitheatre)

48. Jill Scott

Following this year's "To Whom It May Concern" — her first album since 2015's "Woman" — the powerful R&B and neo-soul singer-songwriter goes back-to-back nights at the Fox. (Aug. 26-27, Fox Theatre)

49. Kesha

She was "Tik Tok" before TikTok was cool. Now Kesha is a pop survivor, touring on the strength of last year's "Period" album. Chromeo and Sizzy Rocket get the party going early. (June 5, Pine Knob)

50. Lionel Richie/ Earth Wind & Fire

Mr. "All Night Long" joins up with Earth, Wind & Fire for a night of nothing but hits. (July 1, Little Caesars Arena)

Also!

Movement

The long-running three-day techno party returns to Detroit's Hart Plaza May 23-25, with headliners Carl Cox, Dom Dolla and Sara Landry leading more than 100 acts on six stages of music. More at movementfestival.com.

Aretha Franklin Amphitheatre

Detroit's riverfront amphitheater kicks off its season June 10 with Boney James and runs through Sept. 4 with country act Justin Moore. Other highlights include Juvenile on June 20, Charlie Wilson on July 25 and Robert Glasper on Aug. 12. More at theareatha.com.

A road trip to Grand Rapids

Looking for an excuse to go to the other side of the state? Grand Rapids' brand new outdoor concert venue, Acrisure Amphitheater, opens May 15 with an opening evening featuring Lionel Richie, the War and Treaty and Brian Vander Ark, and its full season includes shows from Jelly Roll (June 13), Dave Matthews Band (July 7 and 8) and Jerry Seinfeld (Aug. 8). More at acrisureamphitheater.com.

search_result.title: The Chicks return to Noblesville at Ruoff after transformative 6 years
search_result.text:
Updated June 14, 2022, 3:46 p.m. ET

Update: An earlier version of this story noted proof of vaccine or a negative COVID-19 test from the past 72 hours was required to enter The Chicks' Ruoff Music Center show on Sunday. That requirement has since been removed from the show.

Not much has changed since The Chicks last played Noblesville's Ruoff Music Center in 2016 — only the name of the venue, the name of the band, the president of the United States (twice), the group's music catalog and the public health status of the entire world.

As the trio prepared for their first tour in five years, that last thing was top of mind.

"Honestly, my nerves are all just based around COVID," lead singer Natalie Maines told IndyStar in a May interview. "I don't want there to be an outbreak on the tour that delays things or cancels things."

Ruoff Music Center: Country music stars The Chicks announce June 19 show in Noblesville

Maines explained The Chicks are taking stricter precautions than most touring acts to ensure the tour unfolds smoothly.

"It's really just an issue of not wanting to cancel concerts," banjo player Emily Strayer added. "For the fans and for us it's just a pain in the butt."

Health concerns aside, the group is particularly excited to tour again on the back of their first studio album in 14 years — 2020's critically acclaimed "Gaslighter." They began May rehearsals with several new band members, reworking old songs and polishing up the new ones.

Maines prepared an early draft of a setlist, which will draw from the band's nearly three decades of bluegrass, country and pop success.

"We have some songs that we've left behind over the years, and sometimes people like those songs and sometimes people don't," Strayer said. "But we're going to play a dice game where we roll the dice, and six songs will be lined up with the numbers on the dice, and whatever it lands on we have to play."

"And songs like (1998's) 'There's Your Trouble' — oldies but goodies — will be on there that we haven't played probably in 25 years," she continued.

Indiana State Fair: 2022 free stage lineup announced, with Kansas leading off

Planning for a massive tour does do certain things to the subconscious, however.

"Emily usually has anxiety dreams — crazy pre-tour anxiety dreams," fiddle player Martie Maguire said of her sister and longtime bandmate. "You haven't had any?"

"Oh, I've had tons," Strayer said. "It's just like an open window, and there's nothing below. And you're standing with your banjo, and the wind's blowing, and like I can't get right. I'm always having those dreams I'm going to fall off the cliff at any moment."

Maines dreamt the band's new hair stylist was driving her and Maguire to a concert in New York City, leaving the two Chicks to do their own hair in the backseat.

The Chicks Tour 2022 will also be, as the name suggests, the group's first since removing "Dixie" from its moniker in 2020.

Maguire explained the group had "cringed" over their name for some time and moved away from it through its merchandising and marketing efforts.

"We picked that name in what, 1989? So it already felt like it didn't suit us," she explained. "And then of course with Black Lives Matter and George Floyd coming to the forefront, it was just embarrassing — downright embarrassing — to have a name like that."

The group has long stood for progressive causes and with the Democratic Party.

Maines famously told a London crowd in 2003 the band did not support the U.S. invasion of Iraq and was ashamed then-President George W. Bush was from Texas, triggering the ire of the country music genre's more conservative artists and fans.

More recently, The Chicks performed "The Star-Spangled Banner" at the 2020 Democratic National Convention.

"Even though our fans know who we are — they know we didn't mean anything negative by that word — we definitely felt the responsibility to hurry up and drop it," Maguire said.

"It felt literally like a shedding of skin and offloading a huge weight for us with who we are," she continued. "But nothing's changed about the show or us as a band."

As such, folks should expect to hear the hits and a good chunk of "Gaslighter" at the Ruoff show.

"We really try to put on a production," Maines said, adding that the band seeks to entertain while showcasing its musicianship. "I know some bands don't do solos anymore, but we're full of solos."

"We always feel the summer outdoor shows people are there to have fun and have a good time."

search_result.text:
Jan. 29, 2026 Updated Jan. 30, 2026, 10:27 a.m. ET

Justin Bieber is returning to the Grammys stage.

For the first time in four years, the "Yukon" singer will perform at the annual award show on Sunday, Feb. 1, the Grammy Awards announced. Bieber, whose album "Swag" is nominated for album of the year and best pop vocal album, plus a best pop solo performance nod for "Daises" and best R&B performance nod for "Yukon," last performed and attended the ceremony in 2022.

Previously announced performers include Olivia Dean, Addison Rae, KATSEYE and Leon Thomas, who will join the full list of best new artists nominees in a new segment at the awards show, as well as nominees Sabrina Carpenter and Clipse, with Pharrell.

Grammys all-time records that could be made or broken in 2026

July's "Swag," a pop and R&B record featuring 21 tracks with three interludes, peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 album charts, while "Daisies" peaked at No. 2 and spent 27 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100. Bieber followed the album with "Swag II" in September.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

Bieber – who last performed his Grammy-nominated track "Peaches" at the award show – has taken a lengthy hiatus from performing, appearing on stage sparingly since revealing in 2022 that he was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Months after the diagnosis, the 31-year-old singer postponed and eventually canceled the remainder of his Justice World Tour dates. That tour also came after a lengthy hiatus, following his 2016-17 Purpose World Tour.

"I performed six live shows, but it took a real toll on me," Bieber said at the time. "So I'm going to take a break from touring for the time being. I'm going to be OK."

Bieber fans will be fed well in 2026, as the "Sorry" singer will also hit the stage at Coachella in his first-ever set when he headlines alongside Carpenter and Karol G in April.

search_result.title: Luke Combs sets a concert attendance record at Lambeau Field
search_result.text:
May 21, 2026, 7:44 p.m. ET

Not only did Luke Combs become the first act to play back-to-back shows at Lambeau Field, he also set a record for the highest attendance for a concert by a single artist in stadium history.

The Green Bay Packers announced a crowd of 51,981 packed Lambeau for the second night of his My Kinda Saturday Night Tour on Saturday, May 16. Combined with attendance of 40,559 for the first concert on Friday, May 15, the two shows drew a total of 92,540 fans.

Combs is only the fifth touring act to play the Green Bay Packers stadium. Both nights also featured guest artists Dierks Bentley, Ty Myers, Jake Worthington and Thelma & James.

Kenny Chesney was the first major act to play the stadium in 2011 for a joint show with co-headliner Zac Brown Band. Attendance was 45,446 that night. Chesney returned in 2015, again for a co-headlining show, this time with Jason Aldean, before a crowd of 53,363. That remains the largest concert crowd ever at Lambeau Field.

Attendance for Billy Joel in 2017 was 45,602. Paul McCartney played to nearly 50,000 in 2019.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

Combs played in-the-round shows on all of his previous U.S. stadium dates on the current tour, which allow for bigger crowds, compared with Lambeau's concert setup of having the stage in the end zone to minimize impact on the playing field.

He set the record for the largest indoor attendance for any concert or event in Nevada history when he played to 70,921 at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas in March. His April 25 concert at Ohio Stadium in Columbus was the largest single-night concert attendance ever at the stadium with 97,367 fans.

Kendra Meinert is an entertainment and feature writer at the Green Bay Press-Gazette. Contact her at 920-431-8347 or kmeinert@greenbay.gannett.com. Follow her on X @KendraMeinert.

search_result.title: Nashville's March 2022 concerts: 14 of the biggest shows in Music City
search_result.text:
Updated Feb. 28, 2022, 1:53 p.m. ET

"Feel It Still." "Bad Guy." "Breaking The Law." "The Less I Know The Better."

You know it's a massive month in Music City when all of those songs — and whatever Bob Dylan feels like playing — are on the collective setlist. Read on to discover 14 of the biggest concerts coming to Nashville this March.

March 1: Alt-J and Portugal. The Man at Nashville Municipal Auditorium

Two of the biggest names in experimental modern rock — one hailing from England, the other from Alaska, and neither from Portugal — have joined forces on a co-headlining tour.

March 3-4: Yola at Ryman Auditorium

The British born, Nashville-based country/Americana phenom is headlining country music's mother church for the first (and second time), with support from another critically hailed transplant, Allison Russell.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

March 6-7: Conan Gray at Ryman Auditorium

The 23-year-old YouTube vlogger-turned-pop star (2020 hit "Heather" is nearing 800 million streams on Spotify) holds a two-night stand at the Ryman on the heels of his latest single, "Jigsaw."

March 8: Jazmine Sullivan at Marathon Music Works

Modern R&B star Sullivan made a big Nashville connection when she performed "The Star-Spangled Banner" with Eric Church at last year's Super Bowl. After having to postpone a string of dates due to COVID, she'll return to her "Heaux Tales" tour, supporting her first album in six years.

March 9: Billie Eilish at Bridgestone Arena

It's been nearly two years since the 20-year-old pop wunderkind was originally supposed to headline our hockey arena. She's spent the pandemic period crafting a celebrated sophomore album and co-writing/performing the latest "James Bond" theme — which earned her first Oscar nomination.

March 16-18: Morgan Wallen at Bridgestone Arena

Country music's newest megastar largely kept out of the spotlight last year after he was filmed using a racial slur. He's now embarking on his first headlining arena tour in support of 2021's record-breaking "Dangerous: The Double Album," and is being greeted by overwhelming demand. He'll hold a three-night stand at Bridgestone Arena this month.

March 16: Slash at Grand Ole Opry House

Before he buried the hatchet with Axl Rose and toured stadiums once again with Guns N' Roses, the iconic guitarist started recording albums and touring with his longtime collaborators, Myles Kennedy and The Conspirators. They're back in action this year, and their tour will bring Slash to the same stage as the Grand Ole Opry.

March 22: Sparks at Ryman Auditorium

The epic journey of this charmingly inscrutable rock duo was vivdly captured by filmmaker Edgar Wright in the 2021 documentary "The Sparks Brothers." They'll explore a twisting 51-year recording career during their Ryman debut.

March 23: Bob Dylan at Ryman Auditorium

He first stepped onto the Ryman stage at the invitation of Johnny Cash in 1969. The mythical singer-songwriter, now 80, returns on the heels of a phenomenal 2020 album, "Rough & Rowdy Ways."

March 23: Judas Priest at Nashville Municipal Auditorium

"Breaking the Law," "You've Got Another Thing Coming," "Painkiller" — if any of those titles kickstart some power chord chugging in you head, you owe to yourself to see these heavy metal godfathers in the flesh.

March 23: Tame Impala at Bridgestone Arena

While a headlining slot at the twice-canceled Bonnaroo didn't come to pass, these neo-psychedelic rockers from Australia will enjoy some arena-sized glory in Nashville during their Bridgestone debut.

March 26: Buddy Guy at Ryman Auditorium

Now 85, the celebrated blues veteran is still going strong — his last album, "The Blues Is Alive And Well," won a Grammy in 2019.

March 27: Casting Crowns at Grand Ole Opry House

The Atlanta-based worship rockers — fronted by youth pastor Mark Hall — released a new album, "Healer," in January. Hit single "Scars in Heaven" is one of several songwriting collaborations between Hall and fellow Christian star Matthew West.

March 31: Mitski at Ryman Auditorium

The acclaimed indie-rocker's Ryman stop is actually an adopted hometown gig. She quietly moved to town two years ago after she finished touring in support of 2018's "Be The Cowboy" — which was named album of the year by Pitchfork and others. She crafted her latest, 2022's "Laurel Hell," at East Nashville's Bomb Shelter studio.
